questions.prompt: An analyst must decide whether a parcel that was dispatched and never delivered counts as late in the on-time rate. The assistant offers to choose "the most common convention". What should the analyst do with this step?
options: Delegate it: a convention is a known right answer that the assistant can look up
Keep it: the choice changes every later number and the analyst must defend it
Delegate it, then ask the assistant to confirm the choice it made in a second request
Skip it: the system flag already encodes a definition, so no decision is needed
questions.explanation: A definition decides every number after it and is a judgement the analyst answers for, so it is kept.
misconceptions: Treats a definition as a fact to look up; the organisation chooses it, and the choice moves the result
A second answer from the same assistant is not an independent check of a judgement
The system flag follows whatever definition was in force and may mix two; it does not decide which one the analysis needs

questions.prompt: A checked table of monthly on-time rates exists. The next step is plotting it as a line chart with labelled axes. Which mark fits, and why?
options: Keep: charts are what readers see first, so the analyst should always draw them by hand
Assist: every chart needs its numbers recomputed another way before anyone reads it
Delegate: an error is cheap to see by reading the axes against the checked table
Keep: plotting code is long and cannot be reviewed in the time a lab or project allows
questions.explanation: The input is already checked and a wrong chart shows when its axes and values are read against the table, so the step can be delegated.
misconceptions: Confuses the importance of a step with whether an error in it is cheap to detect
The numbers were already checked; the chart needs its encoding read, not a recomputation
Plot code is short and its output is inspected directly

questions.prompt: Two steps of a plan: (a) renaming columns to the team's naming style, (b) joining deliveries to route plans to compare long and short routes. An analyst marks both "delegate". What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: both steps are code, and code is what assistants write well
Step (a) should be kept, because column names matter to every reader of the result
Both should be kept, because any join can fail and any rename can break later code
Step (b) can multiply rows silently, so its row counts need the analyst's check
questions.explanation: A join can fan out and change a rate with no error message, so the step is drafted by the assistant and checked by the analyst.
misconceptions: Sorts by the kind of work, not by what an undetected error would cost
A rename changes no number and its diff is read in a minute
Keeping everything gives up the help where an error is cheap to catch

questions.prompt: Which pair of questions best decides whether an analysis step can be delegated to an assistant?
options: How costly is an undetected error, and how cheaply can I detect one?
How long would the step take me, and how fast is the assistant?
Is the step code or prose, and which does the assistant do better?
Did the assistant do this step well last time, and is the model recent?
questions.explanation: Delegation depends on the cost of an error that slips through and on how cheaply the result can be verified.
misconceptions: Time saved says nothing about whether a wrong result would be noticed
The form of the output does not tell how much an error would cost
Past success on one run does not bound the error on this one

questions.prompt: An assistant answers "What is our on-time rate?" with "85.3%" and a query that joins deliveries to scans and averages the system flag. What does the single number hide?
options: Only rounding: the query is the definition, and a query that is shown hides nothing else
A syntax problem in the join that the notebook would have reported when the cell ran
Several unstated choices: the definition, the denominator and which parcels were counted
Nothing, provided the query ran without an error and the number is in a plausible range
questions.explanation: A one-line request leaves the definition, the population and the denominator open, and the assistant filled each one silently.
misconceptions: Takes the query for the definition; the query embodies choices nobody made on purpose
The query runs; the problem is in what it means
A query that runs can still count the wrong parcels

questions.prompt: A brief asks for "the monthly on-time rate for the last year". Which acceptance check can a reviewer apply without asking the author?
options: The result looks reasonable for a courier of this size and matches what the team expects
The assistant confirms in its reply that it followed every instruction of the brief
The code is well commented, runs without errors and uses the tables named in the brief
The parcels counted in all months add up to the dispatched parcels of real customers
questions.explanation: A check must be something a reviewer can compute and compare: a total that must reconcile is one.
misconceptions: "Reasonable" has no threshold a reviewer can apply
The assistant's statement about itself is not evidence
Running and readable code can still count the wrong rows

questions.prompt: The definition of on time changed in April. A brief for a full-year trend must say which of the following?
options: Use the system's on-time flag for every month
Apply one named definition to every month, computed from the timestamps
Report the months before and after April in two separate charts
Let the assistant choose the definition and state its choice
questions.explanation: A trend across a definition change is comparable only when one stated definition is applied to all months.
misconceptions: The flag follows the definition in force, so the series jumps at the change
Splitting the chart hides the break without making the months comparable
Stating a choice does not make it the organisation's definition

questions.prompt: A reply to a brief returns a monthly rate on 496,046 parcels. The brief's check says the total must equal the 486,078 dispatched parcels of real customers. What is the most likely cause?
options: Duplicated rows from a join to scans
A rounding difference between engines
Cancelled orders were left in the denominator
Two months were dropped by a date filter
questions.explanation: The total is about ten thousand too high, which is the size of the cancelled orders that the brief excludes.
misconceptions: A join to scans would add tens of thousands of rows, and duplicates concentrate in two months
Rounding cannot add ten thousand parcels
A dropped month would make the total smaller, not larger

questions.prompt: What belongs in a project context file such as AGENTS.md, and not in the brief for one request?
options: The question the director asked this week, word for word
The grain of each table and the standing definitions
The acceptance checks written for this one request
The headline numbers that the last analysis reported
questions.explanation: The context file carries what holds for every request in the project: grain, keys, definitions and rules.
misconceptions: The question belongs to one request, so it goes in the brief
Checks are written for one request and its result
Past results can anchor the assistant and are not rules of the project

questions.prompt: With a context file, an assistant's rate moved from 7.3 points away from the reference to 2.5 points away. What should the analyst conclude?
options: The context file works, so the acceptance checks can be dropped from later requests
The context file made no real difference, because the reply is still not on the reference
The remaining gap of 2.5 points is ordinary noise between two runs of the same request
Context narrows the gap; the acceptance checks are still needed to find what remains
questions.explanation: A context file reduces wrong assumptions and does not remove them; the checks found a denominator that was still wrong.
misconceptions: Takes an improvement for a guarantee
A gap cut by two thirds is a real difference
The gap has a cause that a check can name: the denominator

questions.prompt: An assistant computed a quarterly rate in pandas. Which check counts as recomputing it another way?
options: Writing the rate in SQL from the raw tables, without reading the assistant's code first
Running the assistant's code again in a fresh kernel and comparing the two outputs
Asking the assistant to explain each line of its code and reading the explanation closely
Asking a second assistant whether the number looks right for a courier in this region
questions.explanation: An independent recomputation uses another route from the raw data, so the same mistake is unlikely to repeat.
misconceptions: The same code repeats the same mistakes
An explanation describes the code and does not test it
A plausibility opinion has no access to the data

questions.prompt: After a join of parcels to route plans, the result has 22,699 rows and 21,158 distinct parcels. What does this show?
options: The join dropped the parcels that have no plan, which lowers the number of distinct parcels
Some parcels matched more than one plan row and are counted more than once
The filter on dates is too narrow and has removed the parcels of the last days
Nothing: rows and distinct keys often differ after a join, and the rate is not affected
questions.explanation: More rows than distinct keys means a fan-out: the join key is not unique on the other side.
misconceptions: Dropped parcels lower both numbers; they do not make rows exceed keys
A date filter removes rows and cannot multiply them
When one row should be one parcel, a difference is a defect

questions.prompt: A query filters created_at BETWEEN '2026-07-01' AND '2026-09-30' on a timestamp column. Which parcels are lost?
options: Those created during 1 July before the hub opens
Those with an empty timestamp, and no other parcel
None: BETWEEN includes both ends of the range
Those created during 30 September after midnight
questions.explanation: The upper bound is read as the first instant of 30 September, so the rest of that day falls outside.
misconceptions: The lower bound at midnight includes all of 1 July
Empty timestamps are lost too, but a whole day of parcels is also dropped
Both ends are included, and the end is an instant, not a day

questions.prompt: A bar chart shows late parcels per week: Riyadh 847, Dammam 464. The text says "Riyadh has the worst lateness problem". Riyadh handles about two and a half times Dammam's volume. What is the right response?
options: Accept the claim: the bars are computed correctly from the deliveries table
Reject the chart: a bar chart is the wrong chart type for showing lateness
Compare late rates: the chart encodes counts, which follow volume
Ask the assistant to change the colours and sort the bars for clarity
questions.explanation: Counts follow volume; the claim is about performance, which needs a rate, and Dammam's late rate is the higher one.
misconceptions: Correct counts can still answer a different question from the one asked
The chart type is fine; the measure is the problem
Styling does not change what is measured

questions.prompt: An assistant summarises "what customers complain about" from the first 500 rows of an export. The export is sorted by channel. What is the main problem?
options: 500 texts are too few for any summary
The first rows of a sorted file are one channel, not a sample of customers
Summaries of text can never be checked
The assistant should have read the texts in the original language
questions.explanation: Rows taken from the top of a sorted export represent the sort order, so shares in the summary cannot be trusted.
misconceptions: 500 random texts would support a rough summary; the selection is the fault
Each sentence of a summary can be tested against counts of labelled categories
Language handling matters, and it is not why the shares are wrong here

questions.prompt: Your SQL recomputation gives 72.3% and the assistant gave 84.3% for the same quarter. What is the next step?
options: Report your own number, since you wrote the query by hand and can explain every line
Average the two numbers and report the mean with a note that sources differ
Ask the assistant which of the two numbers is right and report the one it chooses
Reconcile: change one difference at a time until one number becomes the other
questions.explanation: A reconciliation names each cause of the gap and its size, which shows which number is right and why.
misconceptions: Your own number may hold the error; a gap is unexplained until reconciled
A mean of a right and a wrong number is wrong
The assistant cannot settle it without the same checks

questions.prompt: The same request is sent five times with the same model and settings. Four runs name Dammam as the worst city and one names Riyadh. What should the analyst look at first?
options: Which measure each run used
Which run has the longest code
Which run finished fastest
Which answer the majority gave
questions.explanation: Runs often differ in the measure chosen; the Riyadh run counted parcels and the others used a rate.
misconceptions: Length of code says nothing about the measure
Speed is unrelated to correctness
A majority can share a wrong measure; the cause of the split must be found

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a conclusion "held in every run"?
options: It is proven correct, since five independent runs reached the same conclusion
The model must have been run at temperature zero, where runs cannot differ
It is stable under this request; it still needs a check against the data
The five runs produced identical code, so the result is one run repeated
questions.explanation: Stability across runs is not correctness: five runs can agree on the same wrong assumption.
misconceptions: Agreement between runs is not evidence about the data
Stability can occur at any temperature
Different code can reach the same conclusion

questions.prompt: Which set of columns makes a variability table useful to a reviewer?
options: Run number, time taken, tokens used, cost of the run, whether the run finished
Run number, code length, model name, number of tables used, number of joins
Run number, similarity score to the first run, temperature, seed, model name
Run number, measure used, headline number, conclusion, supported by the data or not
questions.explanation: The table must let a reader see what each run measured, what it concluded and whether the data supports it.
misconceptions: Cost and time do not show whether the runs agree
Neither field describes the result of a run
Similarity of code is a hint, not the comparison of conclusions

questions.prompt: Two runs produce code that is 37% similar and the same headline number. Two others are 82% similar and differ by three points. What does code similarity tell you?
options: Similar code means similar results
Little by itself: results must be compared directly
Dissimilar code is always the wrong one
The similarity score should replace the headline comparison
questions.explanation: Different code can agree and similar code can differ in one decisive line, so numbers and conclusions are compared directly.
misconceptions: One changed filter in similar code can move the number
A different route to the same number is a form of confirmation
Similarity measures text, not meaning

questions.prompt: A colleague wants to repeat your variability measurement next month. Which logged items does that need beyond the request?
options: The names of the five output files and the folder they were saved in
Your notes on which of the five runs you liked best, and why
The model, its settings and the context file's fingerprint
A screenshot of the notebook taken after the fifth run
questions.explanation: To repeat a measurement of run-to-run variation, the model, its settings and the context in force must be known.
misconceptions: File names do not describe the conditions of the runs
A preference is not a condition of the experiment
A screenshot cannot be rerun

questions.prompt: A table has sixteen operational columns, a district column and a recipient phone column. Under a policy where a table takes the level of its most sensitive column, how is it handled?
options: As Public: most columns are operational
As Public once the phone column is hidden in the notebook
As two tables with two levels
As Restricted personal data: its rows do not go to a hosted assistant
questions.explanation: Two personal columns set the level of the whole table, whatever the other columns hold.
misconceptions: The level follows the most sensitive column, not the majority
Hiding a column on screen does not change what the table holds
The level is assigned to the table as stored

questions.prompt: For two days the labs sent requests about a Restricted table to a hosted model. Why was that within the policy?
options: Only table and column names were sent; no row left the notebook
The data was pseudonymised first, so the rows were no longer personal
Free hosted models do not store the prompts that they receive
The table was reclassified as Public for the length of the course
questions.explanation: The policy lets the schema of any table be shown; the model wrote code that ran locally on the rows.
misconceptions: Nothing was pseudonymised, and that would not open the hosted route
What a service stores is not something the analyst can rely on or verify
The level did not change; what was sent did

questions.prompt: An aggregate counts complaints by district and category; its smallest cell holds 4 complaints. May it go to a hosted assistant?
options: Yes: an aggregate is a summary, and summaries are not personal data under any policy
Yes, provided the district names are replaced by codes before the table is sent
No: it has a column locating people and cells small enough to describe them
No: aggregates built from a Restricted table may never leave, whatever they hold
questions.explanation: An aggregate is safe to share only without columns that locate a person and without small cells, and when its owner classifies it Public.
misconceptions: Small cells with a location can describe identifiable people
Translation does not change what the cells reveal
An aggregate with no personal column and large cells can be classified Public by its owner

questions.prompt: A colleague masks every phone number in the complaint texts with a pattern and wants to send the texts to a hosted assistant. What is the right answer?
options: Agree: with the phone numbers masked, the personal data is gone from the texts
Refuse: names and what a person wrote remain, so the level is unchanged
Agree, on condition that only the texts written in English are sent
Refuse: masked text cannot be analysed by any assistant, hosted or local
questions.explanation: Masking one kind of identifier lowers the harm of a leak and leaves free text by a person at its level.
misconceptions: A pattern finds numbers and misses names and other details
The language of a text does not change its level
Masked text can be analysed, on a local assistant or by people

questions.prompt: A table of drivers holds a government identity number. A guard written from the policy receives a request to send its rows to a local assistant. What should it do?
options: Allow: a local assistant never leaves the organisation
Allow after logging the request
Ask the analyst to confirm, then allow
Block and name the rule: this table goes to no assistant
questions.explanation: The policy sends a table with a government identity number to no model; analysis uses a view without the column.
misconceptions: Local lowers exposure, and the policy still excludes this table
Logging records a breach and does not prevent it
A guard that an analyst can click through is a reminder, not a control

questions.prompt: A screen for the local assistant's replies is run on twelve replies whose verdicts are known. Five carry a mobile written 05 and eight digits, two carry one written with +966, five carry none. It masks the five, lets the two through unchanged and flags none of the clean five. What do you decide?
options: Not ready: fix the +966 form, then rerun the screen on all twelve replies
Ready: it caught most numbers and raised no false alarm on clean text
Ready, provided each alert quotes the number so that a person can check it
Not ready, and never will be: a screen must find every name in a reply
questions.explanation: A screen is trusted when every known case gets its verdict; a missed form is fixed and the whole set is run again, clean cases included.
misconceptions: Two personal replies passing unchanged is a leak, whatever the share caught
An alert that quotes the value spreads the personal data it was meant to stop
A screen is tested on the identifiers it claims to find; names are why replies built from texts stay local

questions.prompt: A log line reads: request "same but by city", code "see notebook cell 14". What can a peer do with it?
options: Rerun it by opening the notebook and running cell 14, as the log line says to do
Rerun it by asking the assistant the same thing and comparing the answer with the report
Nothing: the request and the code point to a conversation and a notebook state that are gone
Rerun it after guessing which model was used from the date on which the log was written
questions.explanation: A log line must stand alone: the full request and the code itself, not pointers to things that change.
misconceptions: The notebook has been edited since; cell 14 is no longer that code
A new request is a new analysis, not a rerun
The model is one missing field among several

questions.prompt: A peer reruns your logged code and gets a different number. The data fingerprints match. What follows?
options: The code or the environment differs; the data did not change
The data was updated between your run and the peer's rerun
The model has changed since your run and now writes other code
The fingerprint is unreliable and should be computed another way
questions.explanation: Matching fingerprints rule out a change in the data, which leaves the code as run or the environment.
misconceptions: A changed table would change its fingerprint
A rerun executes logged code and does not call the model
A match is exactly the information the fingerprint exists to give

questions.prompt: Every logged step of a package reruns to its logged value. The README states a number that no step produces, and the peer believes it is correct. What does the rerun log say?
options: Reproduced: every step reran
Not reproduced: one headline number has no logged step
Reproduced: the peer confirmed the number from experience
Reproduced, with a note for next time
questions.explanation: Reproduced means the headline numbers are reached from the package; a number with no step rests on the author's word.
misconceptions: Readers quote the README, so the README is what must be reached
A peer's belief is not a rerun
A note does not change the fact that the number cannot be reached

questions.prompt: A log shows three assisted steps; one, a chart, has no verification. Which disclosure sentence is honest?
options: All numbers in this report were verified by the analyst before publication
AI tools assisted with minor formatting of the tables and charts in this analysis
Two steps were verified as described; the chart was not verified and is illustrative
An assistant drafted the quarterly rate and the route comparison, both verified
questions.explanation: A disclosure is tested against the whole log: it names each step and says how far each was checked.
misconceptions: The log has no check for the chart, so the sentence is false
Understates assistance on headline numbers and names nothing
True in every word, and misleading by leaving the chart out

questions.prompt: A README says 68.4% and the logged step that it cites gives 68.1%. What is the best prevention for next time?
options: Write the README's numbers from a file that names each number's step and key
Round every number in the README to whole percentages, so small changes vanish
Ask a second peer to proofread the README against the log before each release
Stop quoting numbers in the README and point readers to the log for every value
questions.explanation: When the text is generated from the log's headline values, it cannot drift from them.
misconceptions: Rounding hides small drifts and not large ones
Proofreading finds some drifts; removing the typing prevents them
Readers need the headline numbers

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for a number that an assistant computed and an analyst verified?
options: The assistant's provider
Nobody: it is a joint product
The reviewer who read the report
The analyst who signs the report
questions.explanation: Verification is how the analyst earns the right to sign; the assistant signs nothing.
misconceptions: A provider does not know the analysis or its definitions
Shared production does not remove the signature
A reviewer checks; the author answers for the work
